project: J. Lieb Foods Industrial Asset Graph — Narrated Presentation
runtimeRule: Never call ElevenLabs from the public GitHub Pages client. Generate narration ahead of time and commit only finished audio/timing assets.

scenes.title: Cold Open — What a Plant Really Runs On
scenes.visual: Black screen into real industrial details: disconnect handle, motor fan, conduit, cabinet latch, VFD display, production line. Presenter emerges in a real industrial environment.
scenes.narration:
[calm, experienced]
Every plant has equipment.

Panels. Motors. Drives. Control cabinets. Conveyors. Sensors. Valves. Miles of wire.

You can put a manufacturer and a model number on most of it.

But that isn't the hardest thing in this building to replace.

[reflective]
The hard part is knowing why it's there.

Where it gets power.
What else depends on it.
What somebody changed ten years ago.
What alarm really means what.
And what you check first... when the line goes down.

[more serious]
That knowledge usually doesn't live in a drawing.

It lives in people.

And people eventually leave.

scenes.title: The Problem — Knowledge Walks Out the Door
scenes.visual: Presenter walks past old panels and production equipment. Overlay old drawings, handwritten notes, phone photos, binders, unlabeled cabinet details. End on silhouette of experienced electrician walking away.
scenes.narration:
[serious, understated]
At J. Lieb Foods, a lot of this facility was built, modified, repaired, and kept running by people who know it from experience.

One of the people carrying a huge amount of that knowledge is an electrician with decades in the trade and years inside this plant.

He knows the production lines because he helped wire them.

He knows which cabinet actually feeds what.
Which modification never made it onto a print.
Which fault looks serious but usually starts with one simple check.
Which spare part matters.
Which machine has a habit nobody would know unless somebody told them.

[pause, reflective]
When that experience retires, the person may leave...

but the plant still needs the knowledge.

If we don't capture it, the next electrician starts paying for it again.

In troubleshooting time.
In wire tracing.
In downtime.
In repeated mistakes.

And sometimes... in the middle of production.

scenes.title: The Answer — Industrial Asset Graph
scenes.visual: Dark blueprint/graph interface grows from Facility node into Area/Line, Cabinet, Machine, Device, Documentation. Presenter gestures toward floating graph relationships.
scenes.narration:
[confident, practical]
That's what the Industrial Asset Graph is meant to solve.

Not another folder full of pictures.

Not another binder that gets set on a shelf.

A living map of the facility's working knowledge.

Start at the facility.

Move into an area or production line.

Open a machine.

Open a control cabinet.

Then drill all the way down to the device that matters.

PLC.
VFD.
Power supply.
Contactor.
Relay.
Terminal block.
Sensor.
Motor.

And from every one of those points, see the relationships around it.

What feeds it.
What it feeds.
Where it is.
What controls it.
What documentation exists.
What has been verified in the field.

[slightly emphatic]
The goal isn't to collect information.

The goal is to make the right information usable... when somebody actually needs it.

scenes.title: Capture Reality — Evidence, Not Guesswork
scenes.visual: Real field photos flow into structured cards. Cabinet photo becomes black-and-white schematic layout. Status badges appear: Verified, Field Verify, Inferred, Disputed, Retired.
scenes.narration:
[matter-of-fact]
The system has to reflect the plant as it actually exists.

That means field photos.

Nameplates.

Cabinet layouts.

Panel and circuit sources.

Voltage and control power.

Device manufacturer, model, and serial information.

VFD parameters.

PLC and I/O information.

Safety devices and interlocks.

Communications.

Procedures.

Troubleshooting notes.

Known weak points.

Undocumented modifications.

And the things an experienced electrician says you need to know before you touch it.

[firm]
And just as important... we don't pretend a guess is a fact.

Information can be marked Verified.

Field Verify.

Inferred.

Disputed.

Or Retired.

That matters.

Because bad documentation with a confident label can be worse than no documentation at all.

scenes.title: Build the Standard — Line 2 Control Cabinet
scenes.visual: Zoom to Line 2. Show control cabinet exterior, then interior image, then schematic-style device placement without conductors. Click cabinet devices individually.
scenes.narration:
[practical, focused]
The way to build a system like this is not to try to document an entire factory in one shot.

You build one piece correctly.

Then make that the standard.

For us, that means taking a control cabinet on Line Two and documenting it deeply enough that somebody else can use it.

Its location.

Its purpose.

Its incoming power.

Its disconnect.

Every major device inside.

Where each device sits in the cabinet.

What the device is.

What it talks to.

What talks to it.

Then we make the cabinet interactive.

Click the cabinet.

See the layout.

Click the drive.

Open the drive record.

Click the PLC.

Open the PLC record.

Click a relay or contactor and see what we've captured about it.

[confident]
Once one cabinet works from top to bottom, we aren't inventing the process anymore.

We're repeating it.

scenes.title: Capture the Human Knowledge
scenes.visual: Presenter beside retiring electrician silhouette / empty workbench. On-screen cards populate: Startup, Shutdown, Reset, Recovery, Recurring Failure, Weak Point, Modification, Critical Spare, Alarm Cause.
scenes.narration:
[warmer, reflective]
The drawings tell us what the system was supposed to be.

The people tell us what happened after that.

That's why this project has another job.

Capture the human knowledge while we still can.

How do you start it?

How do you shut it down?

How do you reset it after a fault?

What usually causes that alarm?

What fails more often than it should?

What modification was made in the field?

What part should already be sitting on the shelf?

What do you check before you spend an hour tracing wires?

And maybe the most important question of all...

[gentle emphasis]
What do you know about this machine that nobody has ever written down?

That's the information that turns documentation into knowledge.

scenes.title: When the Line Stops
scenes.visual: Production scene freezes, warning light pulses, sound drops. UI search opens. User navigates Line 2 → Cabinet → Device → Troubleshooting/relationship record. Presenter remains calm.
scenes.narration:
[serious, controlled]
Now picture the reason this matters.

It's two in the morning.

A line stops.

The person who normally knows that machine isn't there.

You can start opening cabinets and tracing conductors.

You can search through old PDFs.

You can scroll through somebody's phone pictures.

You can call somebody at home.

Or...

you can open the asset graph.

Find the line.

Find the cabinet.

Find the device.

See the power source.

See the relationships.

See the field photo.

See the last known notes.

See the known failure.

See the reset or recovery procedure.

[pause]
That doesn't replace a good electrician.

It gives the good electrician a better starting point.

And in maintenance... a better starting point can save a whole lot of time.

scenes.title: What We Are Actually Building
scenes.visual: Fast cinematic montage: building map, service entrance H1/H2/H3, gutters, cabinet nodes, machine records, photos, diagrams, search, relationship graph.
scenes.narration:
[confident, building momentum]
So this project is bigger than a website.

We're building a facility memory.

A map that connects the physical plant to the electrical system, controls, machines, devices, documents, procedures, and field experience behind them.

A place where a service entrance can connect to its downstream equipment.

A cabinet can connect to its devices.

A machine can connect to its procedures.

A component can connect to its replacement information.

A photograph can connect to the exact asset it proves.

And a technician can move through those relationships without already knowing where the answer is hidden.

[measured]
It will never be finished in the sense that a plant is never finished.

Equipment changes.

People learn things.

Modifications happen.

The graph changes with it.

That's why it is a live system.

scenes.title: Closing — Leave the Knowledge Behind
scenes.visual: Presenter stands still in facility. Plant continues operating behind him. Graph lines slowly illuminate equipment. Finish on title card: J. LIEB FOODS · FACILITY KNOWLEDGE · LIVE SYSTEM / INDUSTRIAL ASSET GRAPH.
scenes.narration:
[reflective, sincere]
A good tradesman fixes the problem in front of him.

A great one leaves the next person with more than he had.

A clear label.

A correct drawing.

A note that saves an hour.

A procedure that prevents a mistake.

An explanation of why something was done the way it was done.

[quietly]
For years, plants have depended on people remembering.

This is a way to stop asking one person's memory to carry the whole facility.

[confident, final]
Capture it once.

Verify it in the field.

Connect it to the equipment.

Keep it alive.

So when experience walks out the door...

the knowledge doesn't have to go with it.

[pause]

J. Lieb Foods.

Facility knowledge.

Live system.

Industrial Asset Graph.
